Education only. Not for diagnosis, treatment or any clinical decision.
:::

## In 60 seconds

Intracardiac echocardiography (ICE) puts a small phased-array ultrasound probe on a catheter inside the heart.
Five ideas explain most of what it can and cannot show. Depth comes from echo time, using one assumed speed of
sound, 1540 m/s [@zhang2026sos]. Depth resolution is half the pulse length, so it improves with frequency. Signal is
lost to attenuation in proportion to frequency and depth; a probe inside the heart is close to its targets, so it
can use the high frequencies that resolve fine detail, and studies report ICE imaging at 7.5–10 MHz
[@morton2003].
The beam is steered by delays across the elements, and elements spaced too far apart create false copies of
it. And each image line waits for its deepest echo, which caps the frame rate. In the EP lab ICE guides
transseptal puncture with less fluoroscopy [@abdalla2026]; against transesophageal echo (TEE), most comparisons
are observational and their certainty is low [@kanniyan2026; @yaser2026].

## From the field

- **Anatomy you cannot map.** With ICE at 7.5–10 MHz, the cavotricuspid isthmus measured 35 ± 6 mm long at end
  systole and 2.7–4.1 mm thick before ablation, with a pouch or recess in 11 of 15 patients
  [@morton2003].
- **Transseptal puncture without fluoroscopy.** In a randomized trial of 43 patients comparing two ICE-guided
  puncture strategies, every procedure was done without fluoroscopy and without complications; one strategy was
  faster at first (8.5 against 12.0 minutes), the other caught up after about 10 cases [@chen2026tsp]. Pooled
  across eight studies, ICE-guided puncture used 2.07 minutes less fluoroscopy than TEE- or fluoroscopy-guided
  puncture, with similar first-pass success and no increase in safety events [@abdalla2026].
- **ICE or TEE.** For AF ablation, a meta-analysis of six studies (4,760 patients, one randomized) found no
  significant difference in complications and shorter fluoroscopy with ICE, with low to very low certainty
  [@kanniyan2026]. For left atrial appendage occlusion, 27 observational studies showed similar success, shorter
  procedures in adjusted analyses, and more pericardial effusions needing intervention with ICE [@yaser2026].
- **Associations in large databases.** In a US readmissions database, ICE was used in 15.7% of 51,129 AF
  ablations and was associated with fewer 90-day readmissions (hazard ratio 0.88) [@deshpande2022]; in a Japanese
  database of VT ablations it was associated with less cardiac tamponade [@kitamura2021]. With pulsed-field
  ablation, a multicenter cohort found no improvement in procedural metrics with ICE [@dellorusso2023].
- **Shells from ICE.** One center compared a deep-learning module that builds the left atrial shell from ICE with
  its earlier manual contouring, in a before-and-after design [@zou2026] (m40).

## Derivations

### Echo time to depth

A pulse leaves the probe, reflects, and returns after time $t$. With speed of sound $c$ the reflector is at depth

$$
z = \frac{c\,t}{2}, \qquad \hat z = z\,\frac{c_{\text{assumed}}}{c_{\text{true}}}
$$ {#eq-m50-range}

where $\hat z$ is the depth the scanner draws when it assumes $c_{\text{assumed}}$ and sound actually travels at
$c_{\text{true}}$. Scanners commonly assume 1540 m/s [@zhang2026sos]; tissue differs, for example calf muscle
measured 1560–1586 m/s in vivo [@xiao2024]. At 1586 m/s a 35-mm isthmus [@morton2003] would be drawn about 1.0 mm
short (lab part A). The error is a fixed fraction of every distance, so it scales with depth.

**Key takeaways**

- Depth is time times an assumed speed; a wrong speed scales every distance.
- Tracked ICE contours placed in 3-D inherit that scale error.

### Axial resolution

The wavelength is $\lambda = c/f$ for frequency $f$. A pulse of $n$ cycles is $n\lambda$ long, and two echoes stop
overlapping when their reflectors are more than half that apart:

$$
\lambda = \frac{c}{f}, \qquad \Delta z_{\text{axial}} = \frac{n\,\lambda}{2}
$$ {#eq-m50-axial}

At 7.5 MHz the wavelength is 0.205 mm, and a 2-cycle pulse (illustrative) separates reflectors 0.21 mm apart; at
10 MHz, 0.15 mm (lab part B). Both are much finer than the isthmus walls ICE measured [@morton2003]. Resolution
across the beam is set by the aperture instead (see steering).

**Key takeaways**

- Shorter pulses and higher frequencies resolve thinner layers along the beam.
- Resolution along the beam and across it are different quantities.

### Attenuation and how deep an image reaches

Attenuation in soft tissue grows roughly in proportion to frequency. With attenuation slope $\alpha$ in
dB/(cm·MHz), a round trip to depth $z$ costs

$$
L = 2\,\alpha\,f\,z \ \text{dB}, \qquad z_{\max} = \frac{B}{2\,\alpha\,f}
$$ {#eq-m50-attenuation}

where $z_{\max}$ is the depth at which the loss uses up a signal budget $B$. Freshly excised myocardium measured
0.52 dB/(cm·MHz) across the fibers and 1.88 along them [@baldwin2007]. With an illustrative 60 dB budget and the
across-fiber value, the reach is 7.7 cm at 7.5 MHz and 5.8 cm at 10 MHz (lab part C). ICE can afford high
frequencies because it sits close to its targets.

**Key takeaways**

- Higher frequency buys resolution and costs depth.
- Attenuation depends on tissue and even on fiber direction.

### Steering a phased array

A phased array of $N$ elements spaced $d$ apart steers its beam to angle $\theta_0$ by firing element $k$ at
position $x_k$ with delay $\tau_k$. Its response in direction $\theta$ is the array factor:

$$
\tau_k = \frac{x_k \sin\theta_0}{c}, \qquad
\mathrm{AF}(\theta) = \frac{1}{N}\left|\sum_{k=0}^{N-1} e^{\,i 2\pi k \frac{d}{\lambda}(\sin\theta - \sin\theta_0)}\right|, \qquad
\sin\theta_m = \sin\theta_0 + m\frac{\lambda}{d}
$$ {#eq-m50-steer}

The array factor is 1 at $\theta_0$ and again at every grating-lobe angle $\theta_m$ ($m = \pm1, \pm2, \ldots$)
that exists; with $d \le \lambda/2$ none exists for any steering angle. Its first null lies $\lambda/(Nd)$ away in
$\sin\theta$, so a wider aperture gives a narrower beam. An echo arriving through a grating lobe is drawn in the
steered direction: a ghost.

::: {.demo #m50-d1 badge="exact"}
```{=html}
<div id="m50-d1-root" class="demo-root" data-demo="m50-d1"></div>
<script type="module" src="../demos/m50-d1-steering.js"></script>
```

**Assumptions**

- Model: @eq-m50-steer for identical point elements in a line, in the far field, at a single frequency; the
  JavaScript is tested against `epml.ice`.
- Element spacing is given in wavelengths, so the result holds at any frequency; the readout converts it to
  millimeters at 7.5 MHz [@morton2003]. Element counts are illustrative, not the specification of any catheter.
- What would change the result: element directivity, apodization (weighting the elements), wideband pulses (which
  smear grating lobes) and delay errors.
:::

**Key takeaways**

- Delays steer the beam; spacing above half a wavelength creates ghosts.
- Lateral resolution comes from the aperture, not the pulse.

### Frame rate

Each line must wait for echoes from the deepest point $D$, a time $2D/c$. A frame of $N_{\text{lines}}$ lines
therefore refreshes at

$$
\mathrm{FR} = \frac{c}{2\,D\,N_{\text{lines}}}
$$ {#eq-m50-frame-rate}

With 96 lines (illustrative), a 4-cm image refreshes about 200 times a second and a 12-cm image about 67 times
(lab part E). Deeper, wider or denser images are slower.

::: {.demo #m50-d2 badge="exact"}
```{=html}
<div id="m50-d2-root" class="demo-root" data-demo="m50-d2"></div>
<script type="module" src="../demos/m50-d2-depth-frame-rate.js"></script>
```

**Assumptions**

- Model: @eq-m50-axial, @eq-m50-attenuation and @eq-m50-frame-rate with the assumed 1540 m/s
  [@zhang2026sos]; the JavaScript is tested against `epml.ice`.
- Attenuation slopes are the myocardial values of @baldwin2007, applied to the whole path; the path in ICE is
  mostly blood, which is not modeled separately. The frequency range follows @morton2003. The 60 dB budget, the
  2-cycle pulse and the line counts are illustrative.
- What would change the result: focusing, parallel receive beams (several lines per transmit), harmonic imaging
  and time-gain compensation, none of which are modeled.
:::

**Key takeaways**

- Depth, lines and frame rate trade against each other.
- A deep, wide image of a fast-moving catheter is the hardest case.

### From planes to a 3-D shell

When the mapping system tracks the ICE catheter, each imaging plane has a known pose, so contours drawn on it
become 3-D points, and a shell can be built from them (m20). In lab part F, planes rotated about the catheter
axis leave gaps that shrink as the plane count grows, while point accuracy is set by contour noise and, through
@eq-m50-range, by the speed of sound. A published comparison of automated and manual ICE shells is a
before-and-after study at one center [@zou2026].

**Key takeaways**

- More planes close the gaps; they do not make each point more accurate.
- A shell is only as good as the tracking, the contours and the assumed speed of sound.

## Clinical correlate

::: {.callout-note title="Pending clinical review"}
This section describes published findings only. It is not guidance for patient care, and it has
not yet been reviewed by an EP physician.
:::

**Where ICE shows up in EP.** Studies describe ICE for transseptal puncture [@chen2026tsp; @abdalla2026],
for guiding AF ablation as an alternative to TEE [@kanniyan2026], for appendage occlusion [@yaser2026], for
imaging anatomy such as the cavotricuspid isthmus [@morton2003], and in VT ablation [@kitamura2021].

**What the evidence is.** The comparisons of ICE with TEE are meta-analyses of mostly observational studies, and
their authors call the certainty low; no significant difference there means imprecision, not demonstrated
equivalence [@kanniyan2026]. Database studies associate ICE with outcomes but cannot separate ICE from the centers
and operators who use it [@deshpande2022; @kitamura2021]. The one randomized trial cited here compares two ways of
using ICE, not ICE against another modality [@chen2026tsp].

**What a reader should ask:**

- **Compared with what?** TEE, fluoroscopy alone, or another way of using ICE.
- **Which outcome?** Fluoroscopy time, procedure time, complications or recurrence.
- **Who did it?** Experience shapes ICE results; one trial reported a learning curve of about 10 cases
  [@chen2026tsp].

## How experts think

Before trusting an ICE image or a number measured on it, ask:

1. **Is the depth right?** It assumes 1540 m/s; real tissue differs [@zhang2026sos; @xiao2024] (@eq-m50-range).
2. **Can it resolve this?** Compare the structure with $n\lambda/2$ along the beam and with the beam width across
   it (@eq-m50-axial, @eq-m50-steer).
3. **Is that echo real?** Grating lobes, side lobes and reverberation draw echoes where nothing is (@eq-m50-steer).
4. **Is it fast enough?** Depth and line count set the frame rate for a moving catheter (@eq-m50-frame-rate).
5. **What does the evidence compare?** ICE against TEE, against fluoroscopy, or ICE used two ways
   [@kanniyan2026; @chen2026tsp].

One sentence to keep: **an ultrasound image is time turned into distance with an assumed speed, through a beam
whose shape you chose.**

## Cheat sheet

| Quantity | Result |
| --- | --- |
| Depth from echo time (@eq-m50-range) | $z = ct/2$; drawn at $z\,c_{\text{assumed}}/c_{\text{true}}$ |
| Axial resolution (@eq-m50-axial) | $\lambda = c/f$; $\Delta z = n\lambda/2$ |
| Attenuation and reach (@eq-m50-attenuation) | $L = 2\alpha f z$ dB; $z_{\max} = B/(2\alpha f)$ |
| Steering (@eq-m50-steer) | $\tau_k = x_k\sin\theta_0/c$; grating lobes at $\sin\theta_0 + m\lambda/d$; none if $d \le \lambda/2$; first null $\lambda/(Nd)$ |
| Frame rate (@eq-m50-frame-rate) | $c/(2DN_{\text{lines}})$ |

**Values used in this module**

| Value | Source |
| --- | --- |
| Assumed speed of sound 1540 m/s | @zhang2026sos |
| Calf muscle 1560–1586 m/s in vivo (example of real tissue) | @xiao2024 |
| ICE imaging frequencies 7.5–10 MHz | @morton2003 |
| Myocardial attenuation 0.52 (across fibers) and 1.88 (along) dB/(cm·MHz) | @baldwin2007 |

**Studies in this module**

| Study | Comparison | Design |
| --- | --- | --- |
| @abdalla2026 | ICE vs TEE or fluoroscopy for transseptal puncture | Meta-analysis, randomized and observational |
| @kanniyan2026 | ICE vs TEE for AF ablation | Meta-analysis, 5 cohorts and 1 randomized trial |
| @yaser2026 | ICE vs TEE for appendage occlusion | Meta-analysis, observational |
| @deshpande2022 | ICE vs none, AF ablation | Administrative database |
| @kitamura2021 | ICE vs none, VT ablation | Administrative database |
| @dellorusso2023 | ICE vs none, pulsed-field ablation | Multicenter cohort |
| @chen2026tsp | Two ICE-guided puncture strategies | Randomized trial |

## Interview questions

Try each question before you open its model answer. In a real interview, say which assumptions you
are making.

**Q1. How does an ultrasound system know how deep a reflector is?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Model answer</summary>

From the echo's round-trip time and an assumed speed of sound: $z = ct/2$ (@eq-m50-range). Systems commonly
assume 1540 m/s [@zhang2026sos]. If the tissue is faster or slower, every depth is scaled by
$c_{\text{assumed}}/c_{\text{true}}$.

</details>

**Q2. What sets axial resolution, and how would you improve it?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Model answer</summary>

Half the spatial pulse length, $n\lambda/2$ (@eq-m50-axial). Shorter pulses (fewer cycles, wider bandwidth) or a
higher frequency improve it; higher frequency costs penetration (@eq-m50-attenuation).

</details>

**Q3. Why can a probe inside the heart use a higher frequency than a probe that must image from far away?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Model answer</summary>

Round-trip loss is $2\alpha f z$ (@eq-m50-attenuation): for the same signal budget, a shorter path allows a
proportionally higher frequency, which gives finer resolution. ICE sits close to its targets; ICE studies report
7.5–10 MHz [@morton2003].

</details>

**Q4. What is a grating lobe, and how is it avoided?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Model answer</summary>

A full-strength copy of the main beam at $\sin\theta_0 + m\lambda/d$ (@eq-m50-steer), which appears when the
elements are spaced more than half a wavelength apart for the steering range used. Echoes from it are drawn in the
wrong direction. Spacing elements at $\lambda/2$ or less prevents it at any steering angle.

</details>

**Q5. How do you narrow the beam of a phased array?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Model answer</summary>

Widen the aperture: the first null is $\lambda/(Nd)$ from the main lobe in $\sin\theta$ (@eq-m50-steer), so more
elements, or a higher frequency for the same aperture, give a narrower beam. On a catheter the aperture is limited
by its diameter.

</details>

**Q6. Your ICE image updates too slowly to follow the catheter. What can you change?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Model answer</summary>

Reduce the depth or the number of lines (narrower sector or coarser line spacing), since the frame rate is
$c/(2DN_{\text{lines}})$ (@eq-m50-frame-rate). Systems that form several receive lines per transmit can raise it
further, at some cost in image quality.

</details>

**Q7. A contour drawn on tracked ICE planes is merged into the map. List its error sources.**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Model answer</summary>

Catheter tracking error, the speed-of-sound scale (@eq-m50-range), contour placement (resolution and noise),
cardiac and respiratory phase, and gaps between planes that must be interpolated (m20). More planes reduce the
gaps but not the per-point error.

</details>

**Q8. What does the evidence say about ICE against TEE for AF ablation?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Model answer</summary>

A meta-analysis of six studies, one randomized, found no significant difference in complications and shorter
fluoroscopy with ICE, with low to very low certainty; the authors note that no difference reflects imprecision,
not equivalence [@kanniyan2026].

</details>

**Q9. A database study links ICE use to fewer readmissions. Does ICE cause that?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Model answer</summary>

Not shown. The association (hazard ratio 0.88 for 90-day readmission [@deshpande2022]) comes from administrative
codes with propensity matching; centers and operators who use ICE may differ in ways the data do not capture. It
generates a hypothesis for a randomized comparison.

</details>

**Q10. Why might ICE help less with some catheters than others?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Model answer</summary>

Because its benefit depends on what else guides the procedure. In a multicenter pulsed-field ablation cohort,
ICE did not improve procedural metrics [@dellorusso2023]; when a catheter is already well visualized by the
mapping system, ICE adds less to navigation and more to safety monitoring. That is a hypothesis to test, not a
finding.

</details>

**Q11. What does ICE show that an electroanatomic map cannot?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Model answer</summary>

Tissue it never touches: wall structure such as isthmus pouches and thickness [@morton2003], and the fossa during
puncture [@chen2026tsp]. The map only knows where the catheter has been and what it recorded.

</details>

**Q12. A structure looks 1 mm shorter on ICE than on CT. Name a physical reason.**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Model answer</summary>

The speed of sound: if the tissue is faster than the assumed 1540 m/s, every distance is drawn shorter in
proportion (@eq-m50-range). At 1586 m/s a 35-mm structure is drawn about 1 mm short. Other reasons include the
cardiac phase of each image and an oblique imaging plane.

</details>

## Code lab

The lab builds the ultrasound essentials from first principles and ends with the published evidence.

| Part | What you do | Data |
| --- | --- | --- |
| A | Echo time to depth, and the speed-of-sound assumption (@eq-m50-range) | published values |
| B | When two echoes stop overlapping (@eq-m50-axial) | our own pulses |
| C | Attenuation and how deep an image reaches (@eq-m50-attenuation) | published attenuation slopes |
| D | Steering, main lobe and grating lobes (@eq-m50-steer) | our own array |
| E | A sector image of the septum, tenting, and frame rate (@eq-m50-frame-rate) | our own phantom |
| F | A 3-D shell from tracked 2-D planes | our own phantom |
| G | Reading the ICE evidence by design | published results |

- **Python notebook:**
  [labs/python/m50_lab.ipynb]({{< var repo.url >}}/blob/main/labs/python/m50_lab.ipynb).
  Run it from the course repository after `pip install -r requirements.txt`, or
  [open it in Google Colab]({{< var repo.colab >}}/blob/main/labs/python/m50_lab.ipynb).
- **Data:** published values as cited; everything else is generated by our own code. No downloads.

Each part ends with **checks**: lines that pass with the code as given. If you change something
and a check fails, that is information, not an error to hide.

## Self-check

Short checks you can do in your head. Open each answer after you have tried it.

**S1. An echo returns after 26 µs. How deep is the reflector at 1540 m/s?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Answer</summary>

$1540 \times 26\times10^{-6}/2 \approx 0.020$ m, or 20 mm (@eq-m50-range).

</details>

**S2. What is the wavelength at 7.7 MHz, assuming 1540 m/s?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Answer</summary>

$1540/7.7\times10^{6} = 0.2$ mm (@eq-m50-axial).

</details>

**S3. With $\alpha$ = 0.5 dB/(cm·MHz) at 10 MHz, what does a round trip to 3 cm cost?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Answer</summary>

$2 \times 0.5 \times 10 \times 3 = 30$ dB (@eq-m50-attenuation).

</details>

**S4. Elements are spaced one wavelength apart and the beam points straight ahead. Where are the grating lobes?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Answer</summary>

At $\sin\theta = \pm 1$, that is ±90° (@eq-m50-steer): at the edge of the field, and they move inward as soon as
the beam is steered.

</details>

**S5. Doubling the image depth at the same line count does what to the frame rate?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Answer</summary>

Halves it (@eq-m50-frame-rate).

</details>

**S6. True or false: adding more tracked planes makes each ICE contour point more accurate.**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Answer</summary>

False. More planes close the gaps between them; per-point accuracy is set by tracking, contour noise and the speed
of sound (lab part F).

</details>

## Literature figures

These figures are worth looking at alongside this module. We link to them instead of copying them:
some licenses do not allow reuse here, and others we could not confirm. Each entry says what to
look for and where this module explains it.

- **ICE-guided transseptal puncture, pooled.** Abdalla and colleagues pool fluoroscopy time, radiation dose and
  safety across eight studies [@abdalla2026; [free full text](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13062762/)].
  This module: clinical correlate.
- **Two puncture strategies.** Chen and colleagues compare two ICE-guided strategies and their learning curves
  [@chen2026tsp; [free full text](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13053152/)]. This module: from the field.
- **ICE or TEE for appendage occlusion.** Yaser and colleagues report adjusted and unadjusted pooled estimates
  [@yaser2026; [free full text](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13217600/)]. This module: clinical
  correlate.

## Further reading

- **Physics.** Speed-of-sound assumptions [@zhang2026sos; @xiao2024]; myocardial attenuation [@baldwin2007].
- **ICE in EP.** Isthmus anatomy [@morton2003]; transseptal puncture [@chen2026tsp; @abdalla2026].
- **Evidence.** ICE against TEE [@kanniyan2026; @yaser2026]; database studies [@deshpande2022; @kitamura2021];
  pulsed-field ablation [@dellorusso2023].
- **Related modules.** m20 for shells from points, m40 for AI-built shells [@zou2026], m49 for the fluoroscopy ICE
  replaces, and m51 for CT, the other source of pre-procedural anatomy.
